meta.description: Not Picasso. The line is Vincent van Gogh's, from an 1885 letter to Anthon van Rappard. The popular wording is a loose later translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am always doing that which I can not do, in order that I may learn how to do it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Picasso. The thought is Vincent van Gogh's, from an 1885 letter to Anthon van Rappard; the Picasso credit surfaced in 1995.

answer.label: Not Pablo Picasso — actually Vincent van Gogh
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely van Gogh’s: in a letter to fellow painter Anthon van Rappard, written at Nuenen on or about 18 August 1885, he wrote — in the Van Gogh Museum’s translation — “But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.” The polished English wording popularly pinned on Picasso is a looser later rendering of that Dutch sentence; the Picasso credit itself has no documented basis and first appears in 1995, decades after his death.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: A later, looser English variant — not the canonical translation

source.excerpt: But I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.
trail: Quote Investigator traced the saying to van Gogh and found the Picasso credit unsupported, first surfacing in a 1995 Usenet post — see “I Am Always Doing What I Can’t Do Yet…” ↗.
The primary source is van Gogh’s letter 528 to Anthon van Rappard, c. 18 August 1885 ↗, where he writes he keeps making what he can’t do yet in order to learn to do it.
Wikiquote files the line under Picasso’s “Misattributed” section ↗, crediting van Gogh’s 1885 letter to van Rappard.
source.excerptNote: The Van Gogh Museum’s modern translation of the Dutch original. The widely shared “I am always doing that which I can not do, in order that I may learn how to do it” is a smoother paraphrase of this same sentence.

sourceLink.text: Read letter 528 at the Van Gogh Museum letters archive

source.rightsNote: The underlying thought comes from van Gogh’s 1885 Dutch letter, whose original text has long been in the public domain. But the exact English wording shown here is an anonymous later variant with no identifiable published translator, so no copyright status can be asserted for it; note that the standard modern English translations (such as the Van Gogh Museum’s 2009 edition) are themselves in copyright.

author.name: Vincent van Gogh
author.heading: About Vincent van Gogh
author.bio: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) was a Dutch painter whose roughly 2,100 works, made in barely a decade, became foundational to modern art. His voluminous letters — above all to his brother Theo and to fellow painters such as Anthon van Rappard — are among the most revealing artist’s writings ever preserved. This line comes from that correspondence, written while he was at work on The Potato Eaters in 1885.

misattribution.heading: How Picasso got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “famous-name magnet” swap: a genuine line by one artist drifts onto a more marketable one. The sentiment is real and really van Gogh’s — only the attribution and the exact wording are off.

items.why: There is no source in Picasso’s writings, interviews, or documented remarks for this line. Quote Investigator ↗ found the earliest Picasso credit only in a 1995 Usenet post — 22 years after his 1973 death — and Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed.

Van Gogh’s actual sentence, in the Van Gogh Museum translation, reads “I keep on making what I can’t do yet in order to learn to be able to do it.” The circulated “that which I can not do … in order that I may learn how to do it” is a smoother, unsourced rendering — see Quote Investigator’s survey of the variants ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The words — and the idea — belong to Vincent van Gogh, written to Anthon van Rappard on or about 18 August 1885 ↗.

context.heading: Why the line rings true for a painter
lead: Van Gogh wrote the sentence at Nuenen in the summer of 1885, in the months around The Potato Eaters, his first ambitious multi-figure canvas. Defending his rough, self-taught approach to van Rappard — who had criticized that very painting — he cast his constant reaching beyond his current skill not as failure but as method: you attempt what you can’t yet do precisely in order to learn it.
That it later attached to Picasso is unsurprising — the idea of the restless artist who works at the edge of his ability fits the popular image of both men. But the documented words are van Gogh’s.
